Flooding Disrupts Industry and Transport Across Belarus as Heavy Rains Continue

Heavy rainfall has led to widespread flooding in Belarus, causing major disruptions to industry, transportation, and daily life across the country. The deluge, which began late Monday, has already swelled rivers and inundated key road and rail links, halting production at several manufacturing plants and threatening further economic fallout as the storm system lingers.

Authorities have declared a state of emergency in parts of the Minsk, Hrodna, and Homiel regions, where water levels continue to rise and evacuation efforts are underway in low-lying villages. The Ministry of Emergency Situations reported that over 2,000 homes have been affected so far, with dozens of families temporarily relocated to community shelters.

"Emergency teams are working around the clock to reinforce embankments and clear blocked drainage systems," said Deputy Minister Aliaksandr Kavalchuk at a press briefing this morning. "Our immediate priority is ensuring the safety of residents and restoring basic infrastructure."

The industrial sector has been particularly hard hit. Giprospetsgaz OAO, a major engineering company, confirmed it has suspended operations at its Zhodzina facility after access roads became impassable and water flooded part of its warehouse complex. "We are assessing the extent of the damage and will resume work as soon as conditions allow," a company spokesperson stated.

Other manufacturers, including the Polesye AgroTech plant in Brest region, have also reported temporary shutdowns due to floodwaters disrupting supply chains and power outages in affected districts.

Rail freight services have been suspended on several main lines, with Belarusian Railways reporting significant delays to both domestic and cross-border cargo. The Belarusian Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates that losses to industrial production and logistics could reach several million rubles if flooding persists through the week.

Local residents expressed concern about the longer-term impact. "This is the worst flooding I remember in twenty years," said Viktar Stankevich, a farmer from the Mogilev region. "We are worried about our fields and whether we can plant this season."

Meteorologists warn that heavy rain may continue through Friday, raising the risk of further disruption. Emergency services have urged the public to follow official updates and avoid non-essential travel in affected regions.
